transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, thank you. Well, what brings me in is that I keep getting these awful doubts that I've missed something important. It happens with all sorts of things, like a number on the mortgage payment, or a clause in a client proof for my design work, or even just a door not being latched. 

And the frustrating thing is, even when I know I checked it, the thought just barges right back in. It always feels like my brain is telling me, what if this is the mistake that costs you everything. It's just become very draining to deal with day to day.
When these doubts come up, do you find yourself going back to recheck things—like re-reading the contract or re-checking the door—over and over, even after you've already confirmed it's fine?

Yes, exactly. I do go back and check. I end up reopening design files over and over, or rereading emails I've already looked at. With bills, I'll keep checking the online payment confirmation just to be absolutely sure. 

Sometimes I even find myself just... saying the figures silently in my head, repeating them until they finally feel settled. It's really impacting my work, honestly. A simple invoice or a minor logo revision can turn into hours of extra checking, and obviously, those are hours I just can't bill for.
Has this kind of checking and doubting always been part of who you are, going back to your teens or twenties, or is this something that started or got noticeably worse more recently?

I don't think it's always been this way, no. I mean, I've always been a careful person—you kind of have to be in design, paying attention to the details. But this constant doubting, where I just can't let it go... I haven't really noticed it being a problem until more recently. It definitely wasn't like this in my twenties. It just seems to have gotten much worse lately, to the point where it's taking up so much of my time.
On an average day, roughly how much total time would you say you spend on this checking and rechecking behavior?

I'm not really sure, honestly. I've never actually timed it or... kept track of the exact hours. 

It happens in bursts throughout the day, so it's hard to add it all up. Like, I'll lose a chunk of time here and there when I'm working on a design file or paying a bill, but... yeah, if you're asking for a total amount of time, I just don't have a specific number for you. It just feels like too much.

You mentioned this got noticeably worse recently—was there anything going on around that time, like a major life change, health issue, or new medication, that seemed to coincide with when the checking got worse?

No, not really. I mean, I've been trying to think back to when it started getting this bad, and... nothing stands out. There wasn't any big event or change in my health. I'm not on any new medications. It just sort of... crept up on me, I guess. I can't point to any specific trigger or life change that happened right before it got worse.
When you feel the urge to recheck something, do you ever try to resist or stop yourself from doing it, and if so, what happens when you try?

I don't think I really try to stop myself, to be honest. I mean... I usually just go ahead and check whatever it is. It feels like the only way to move on with what I'm doing. 

So, I haven't really tested what would happen if I completely tried to resist it. I just... I just do it so I can get back to my work.

When you're in the moment checking something, do you feel like this level of checking is excessive or not really necessary, or does it feel like a reasonable and appropriate thing to do given the risk of a mistake?

I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest. When I'm right in the middle of it... I don't really stop to think about whether it's excessive or not. 

I just feel like I need to be absolutely sure the file is right or the bill is paid, so I just do it. I guess I haven't really stepped back to judge if it's reasonable while it's actually happening. It just feels like something I have to do right then so I can move on.
When you're not in the middle of checking—like later that evening or the next day—looking back, do you feel the amount of checking you did was excessive or unreasonable?

You know, I haven't really thought about it like that. Once I'm finally done for the day and step away from my computer, I... I just try to put it all out of my mind. I don't really look back in the evening and analyze how much I was checking things. So, I guess I don't really have a good answer for that. I just don't really dwell on it after the fact.

Aside from the checking situations you've described, do you find yourself excessively worrying about other things in your life—like your health, relationships, or finances in general—even when there's no specific task to check or recheck?

No, not really. I mean... I have normal worries like anyone else, I suppose, but nothing excessive. It really is just focused on my work and making sure those specific tasks are done right. When I'm not doing that, I don't sit around stressing about my health or my relationships or anything like that.
Aside from the urge to check things, do unwanted thoughts or images—like a sudden mental image of a disaster happening because you missed something—pop into your head and feel hard to push away?

Yeah, that's exactly it. That's actually what brought me in to see you. I keep getting these awful doubts that I've missed something important. 

It could be a number on the mortgage payment, or a clause in a client proof for my design work, or even just a door not being latched. And the thing is, even when I know I just checked it, the thought just barges right back in. It just hits me with... well, what if this is the mistake that costs you everything? So, yeah, those thoughts are very hard to push away.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent, intrusive, distressing thoughts of having made a critical error (obsessions) that are experienced as unwanted and difficult to suppress. These obsessions are directly linked to repetitive checking and rechecking behaviors (compulsions)—re-reading contracts, reopening design files, repeatedly verifying payment confirmations, and mentally repeating figures—performed to reduce the distress caused by the intrusive doubts. The compulsions are time-consuming and have caused clear functional impairment (lost billable work hours, difficulty completing tasks). The pattern is not better explained by generalized anxiety (worry is restricted to specific checking-related content, not diffuse life worries) or by health anxiety (concerns are not focused on illness/bodily symptoms). Insight is partial/uncertain (patient does not clearly recognize the checking as excessive in the moment or in retrospect), consistent with OCD with fair to poor insight. This clinical picture meets criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42).
